title_full: Symphony No. 7 in A major, Op. 92

composer.name: Ludwig van Beethoven
composer.nationality_note: Grove calls him German. He was born in Bonn, then capital of the Electorate of Cologne, and lived in Vienna from 1792 until his death; no German state existed in his lifetime.

era_note: Kept Classical deliberately (decided 21 Aug 2026). periods.json buckets by year and the bucket sets the card colour; Romantic begins 1830, so all nine read Classical. The boundary is global, so moving it to split Beethoven would carry Haydn's late symphonies and the whole of Schubert across with him. Grove's three periods (first to c1802, second to c1812, third 1813-27) divide the nine 1-2 | 3-8 | 9, so the scholarly break falls at the Eroica, not at any date in the 1830s. Second period — Romantic in ambition, Classical in method.

place.note: Wikipedia places the writing at the Bohemian spa where Beethoven was taking the cure. Grove confirms the 1811–12 span and repeated visits to Teplitz 'to take the cure', and that he 'completed it in the spring of 1812, going on without a break to the Eighth Symphony'.

reason.summary: Premiered at a charity concert for soldiers wounded at the Battle of Hanau.
reason.occasion: A charity concert for Austrian and Bavarian soldiers wounded at Hanau, eighteen months after the symphony was finished.
reason.detail: Grove records that the piano and duet arrangements were dedicated separately to Elisabeth Aleksiev, Empress of Russia. Wikipedia describes the premiere: an orchestra led by Ignaz Schuppanzigh that included Hummel, Meyerbeer and Salieri among the players, with Wellington's Victory sharing the programme. Beethoven called it 'one of my best works' at the premiere.

first_performance.ensemble: Ad hoc orchestra led by Ignaz Schuppanzigh
first_performance.reception: The Allegretto was encored on the spot.
first_performance.notes: Grove gives the date; the venue and the players come from Wikipedia. Wellington's Victory was the crowd-pleaser on the bill.

listen_for.hook: The Allegretto: one rhythm, repeated, thickening every time round.
listen_for.detail: Encored at the premiere and detached for separate performance ever since. Grove points to 'the 6-4 chords spanning the Allegretto' as part of the work's reach for new ground.

listen_for.hook: Wagner called it the apotheosis of the dance, and meant the pounding.
listen_for.detail: Grove: 'the expanding introduction, the 6-4 chords spanning the Allegretto, the rolling ostinatos at the ends of the outer movements, the rhythmic preoccupation throughout.'

listen_for.hook: The finale reaches fff — a marking he almost never used.
listen_for.detail: Wikipedia notes the rare fortissimo fortissimo fortissimo in the last movement.
